INSIDE WINNING THE WAIT

A journey in six parts

Follow Quentin Lineworth from the everyday mysteries of waiting to the managerial insights and analytical tools that can help improve service operations.

Part IPart IIPart IIIPart IVPart VPart VI
Table of Content
PART I · Chapters 1–3

Queues Run the World

Queues are everywhere—even when we cannot see them. This opening part introduces the author's journey from an impatient customer to a researcher of waiting lines, then brings Quentin Lineworth onto the scene. Through familiar experiences at stores, airports, hospitals, and digital services, readers discover that queues are much more than everyday inconveniences. They influence how we spend our time and money, make decisions, and experience services; they affect our health and well-being; and, on a much larger scale, they shape the performance of businesses, economies, and entire societies.

PART II · Chapters 4–8

Cracking the Code of Waiting

Why do queues form, and why can they grow so quickly? Quentin introduces Randomizer and Chain Master, the villains representing variability and dependence. Readers discover how these forces interact with high utilization, why safety capacity protects service systems, and how Little’s Law connects three important numbers: how fast customers flow through the system, how many customers are in the system, and how long they spend there. The result is a clearer way to explain—and measure—the causes of congestion.

PART III · Chapters 9–13

The Queue Clinic: Symptoms, Diagnoses, and Cures

Before fixing a troubled queue, managers need a diagnosis. In this part, Quentin plays queue doctor, looking for warning signs in customer feedback, staff experiences, operational data, social media, and financial performance. He examines the arrival and service processes to uncover root causes, then introduces CALM strategies for managing arrivals and SMASH strategies for strengthening service operations. The emphasis is on treating the underlying problem, not merely its symptoms.

PART IV · Chapters 14–16

Queue Architecture: From Fixing to Designing

Rather than repairing queues after problems emerge, why not design better systems from the start? This part shifts from diagnosis to architecture. Quentin explores how economies of scale can absorb variability, how pooling can help resources and customers share capacity, and how priority rules can balance operational performance with fairness. Readers see how thoughtful system design can prevent congestion before it begins.

PART V · Chapters 17–19

Perceived Time: Designing the Experience of Waiting

A shorter actual wait does not always feel shorter. This part moves beyond the stopwatch to the psychology of waiting, where expectations, uncertainty, boredom, fairness, and a sense of control shape customer experience. Quentin introduces Time Bender, the villain who distorts perceived time, and explores practical ways to make waits feel shorter and more tolerable—even when the actual waiting time remains unchanged.

PART VI · Chapter 20

Every Good Guess Deserves a Number

The final part turns intuition into something managers can test. Quentin introduces Q-Analyzer, a tool for exploring waiting times, queue lengths, throughput, and service levels. By changing assumptions about arrivals, service variability, and capacity, readers can examine how the villains influence performance and compare possible improvements. The closing lesson is simple: good managerial judgment becomes stronger when intuition is challenged by numbers, alternatives are systematically compared, and decisions are guided by evidence.

From understanding queues to improving them

The six parts connect everyday observations, operational principles, customer experience, and quantitative analysis into a practical way of thinking about waiting.
